title: The Classical Arrangement
short: The classical oration: introduction (exordium), background (narratio), the claim and its parts (partitio), proof (confirmatio), answers to objections (refutatio) and conclusion (peroratio).
trouble: Learners think there is one fixed order for an argument. The classical parts are a toolkit: writers move the refutation earlier or later to suit the audience.

blocks.html: Where should the concession and rebuttal go? Classical rhetoric had an answer, and a flexible one. Roman teachers such as Cicero, in his early book De Inventione (about 84 BC), described six parts of a persuasive speech.

head: Part
Its job
In an essay
rows: win the audience’s attention and goodwill
a hook and a reason to care
tell the background the audience needs
context: what is happening and why it matters
state the claim and the points to come
the thesis, sometimes with a preview
sum up and move the audience
why it matters; what to do next

blocks.name: wr-essay
blocks.cap: The six parts as an essay map.

blocks.html: The classical parts are a toolkit, not a fixed order. Writers move the refutation earlier for a skeptical audience, shorten the background for experts, and fit the order to the audience and the occasion.

Each part answers a question an audience brings: Why should I listen? What is going on? What exactly are you claiming? Why believe it? What about the objections? So what? Answer them in the order your audience will ask them.

blocks.title: The partitio in the Federalist
blocks.q: Madison, Federalist No. 10: “There are two methods of curing the mischiefs of faction: the one, by removing its causes; the other, by controlling its effects.” Which part of the arrangement is this?
steps: The sentence divides the subject into two parts and tells readers what is coming.
Madison goes on to reject the first method and argue for the second.
Dividing the question and previewing the points is the partitio.
blocks.a: A partitio: it divides the question and maps the argument ahead.

blocks.title: Moving the refutation
blocks.q: You are writing to a school board that has already voted down a later start once. Where should the refutation go?
steps: This audience starts out skeptical, with its objections fresh in mind.
If you wait until the end to answer them, they may stop listening.
Answer the main objection early, right after the background, then give your proof.
blocks.a: Early, before the proof: a skeptical audience needs its objections answered first.

blocks.html: Thinking there is one fixed order for an argument. The classical list is a set of jobs, not a script. Check: who is your audience, and which question will they ask first? Start there.
